content: 1. Efavirenz levels may increase when St. John’s Wort is discontinued, necessitating potential dose adjustments for efavirenz. The enzyme-inducing effects of St. John’s Wort can persist for at least two weeks after stopping its use. 2. Etravirine and products containing St. John’s Wort should not be co-administered. Co-administration can lead to significant reductions in etravirine plasma concentrations, potentially resulting in a loss of therapeutic efficacy. 3. Co-administration of St. John’s Wort with nevirapine is contraindicated, as it is expected to substantially decrease nevirapine concentrations, potentially leading to suboptimal drug levels. If a patient is already taking St. John’s Wort, nevirapine levels and, if possible, viral load should be monitored, and St. John’s Wort should be discontinued. Nevirapine levels may increase after stopping St. John’s Wort, and dose adjustments may be required. The enzyme-inducing effects of St. John’s Wort may persist for at least two weeks after cessation. 4. Co-administration of St. John’s Wort with rilpivirine is contraindicated, as it may significantly reduce rilpivirine plasma concentrations. 5. For individuals with unknown HIV status, HIV testing should be conducted in accordance with national guidelines. 6. Tuberculosis (TB) suspicion in adults and adolescents living with HIV is defined by the presence of symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. In children living with HIV, TB suspicion includes poor weight gain, fever, current cough, or a history of contact with a TB case. 7. Danger signs in suspected TB cases include a respiratory rate greater than 30 breaths per minute, a temperature exceeding 39°C, a heart rate over 120 beats per minute, or an inability to walk unaided. 8. For suspected extrapulmonary TB, appropriate specimens (e.g., cerebrospinal fluid, lymph nodes, or other tissues) should be collected for Xpert MTB/RIF testing. However, Xpert MTB/RIF has low sensitivity for pleural fluid, and data are limited for stool, urine, or blood samples. 9. If Xpert MTB/RIF indicates rifampicin resistance, treatment for multidrug-resistant TB should be initiated. For individuals at low risk of rifampicin resistance, a second Xpert MTB/RIF test should be performed on a fresh specimen. Samples should also be referred for culture and additional drug sensitivity testing. 10. Further TB investigations may include chest X-rays, clinical assessments, and repeat Xpert MTB/RIF testing using fresh specimens. If extrapulmonary TB is suspected, additional specimens should be collected for culture, and abdominal ultrasound may be performed. 11. If Xpert MTB/RIF is unavailable, acid-fast bacillus (AFB) microscopy should be conducted. AFB-positive cases are defined as having at least one positive smear, while AFB-negative cases require two or more negative smears. 12. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (excluding fluoroquinolones) should be used for bacterial infections in suspected TB cases. 13. Diagnosed TB cases should be treated promptly, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) and co-trimoxazole preventive therapy should be provided as appropriate. 14. Facility-specific infection control plans, including TB infection control, should be documented and implemented. A designated person or committee should oversee infection control practices, and all clinical staff should receive documented training in TB infection control within the past two years. 15. Patients with a cough should be identified upon arrival, educated on cough etiquette, separated from others, and fast-tracked through waiting areas, consultations, and investigations. 16. Facility design and patient flow should align with infection control plans, ensuring well-ventilated waiting areas and designated spaces for sputum collection, preferably outdoors. 17. Diagnosed TB cases requiring hospitalization should be isolated or grouped based on drug sensitivity status in rooms with adequate ventilation or negative pressure. 18. Personal protective equipment, such as respirators, should be readily available and used by staff, particularly during high-risk aerosol-generating procedures or when caring for patients with multidrug-resistant or extensively drug-resistant TB. 19. HIV testing should be offered to all individuals with presumptive TB, and time to ART initiation should be evaluated for those testing HIV-positive. 20. Rapid diagnostic tests, such as Xpert MTB/RIF, should be the first-line diagnostic tool for TB in people living with HIV. 21. A tracking mechanism should monitor the turnaround time from TB screening to diagnosis and from diagnosis to treatment initiation, ensuring timely care. 22. The median time between screening positive for TB symptoms and diagnosis should not exceed one day, and the time between diagnosis and treatment initiation should also be no more than one day. 23. HIV and TB prevention and care packages should be available for facility staff, including confidential HIV testing, post-exposure prophylaxis, ART, and isoniazid preventive therapy for staff living with HIV. 24. Decision-making processes for implementing new recommendations should consider equity in access, alignment with epidemiological settings, and contextual issues such as poverty, stigma, and legal barriers. Stakeholders, including healthcare providers, civil society, and government partners, should be involved in the decision-making process.
